title: Heat protectant: what it does and what it does not
meta_description: How heat protectant actually works, what temperature to use on your hair type, and why applying it evenly matters more than which brand you buy.
excerpt: It raises the temperature your hair can survive. It does not make heat damage impossible, and how evenly you apply it matters more than the brand.
intro: Heat protectant is one of the few hair products with a measurable, physical job. It is also one of the most misunderstood — it buys you a margin, not immunity, and most people undermine it by applying it badly.

sections.heading: What it actually does
paragraphs: Heat protectant works by slowing the rate at which heat transfers into the hair shaft. Silicones and film-forming polymers coat the strand, so the hair reaches a lower peak temperature than the tool is set to and gets there more slowly.

That margin is real but finite. A protectant does not let you run a straightener at maximum with no consequence. It gives you room to work at a sensible temperature without damage accumulating as fast.

sections.heading: Temperature matters more than product
paragraphs: The dial on your tool is the single biggest factor in whether your hair survives. Fine, light-coloured or previously bleached hair needs noticeably lower settings than coarse, virgin hair.
Most people can achieve what they want well below the maximum setting. If you are running a tool at its highest setting on every pass, no protectant is going to save the hair.

sections.heading: Application is where it goes wrong
paragraphs: A protectant only protects the hair it touched. Spraying at the front of your head and running a straightener over the back is the most common mistake, and it is why people conclude the product does not work.
Section your hair, mist evenly, then comb through so the product is distributed along the strand rather than pooled where you sprayed.

steps.title: Start on damp or dry hair
steps.detail: Check the label. Blow-dry primers go on damp hair; straightener and curler sprays usually go on dry hair.
steps.tip: Never use a hot tool on soaking wet hair — the water boils inside the shaft.

steps.title: Mist evenly, in sections
steps.detail: Work in four sections. Hold the bottle about 20cm away so it lands as a mist rather than a wet patch.
steps.tip: More product is not better. Saturated hair takes longer under heat, which is worse.

steps.title: Comb it through
steps.detail: This is the step people skip and it is the one that matters most. Combing distributes the film along every strand.

steps.title: Let it dry, then apply heat
steps.detail: Wait until the hair is no longer damp from the spray before the tool touches it.
steps.tip: Fewer, slower passes damage less than many fast ones.

faqs.q: Do I need to reapply between styling passes?
faqs.a: Within one styling session, no. The film is still there. Reapply when you next wash and restyle.
Silicone-based ones can over time, particularly on fine hair. A clarifying wash every few weeks handles it.
No. Bonding and protein treatments can improve how damaged hair looks and behaves, but the structural damage does not reverse. The only real fix is prevention and growing it out.
